A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original classifier-training and certification experiments on CIFAR-10, Imagenette, and HAM10k, including appendix sensitivity experiments.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on the retained datasets and full ImageNet, plus additional comparisons, certification analyses, and classwise error results.

M1.justification: v2 explicitly applies the standard-radius loss to non-sensitive examples for seedwise matrices and all examples for pairwise matrices. v1 Equation 2 uses all examples universally, but its accompanying prose already describes the pairwise distinction. The PDFs therefore leave unclear whether this corrects inconsistent documentation or changes training. Algorithm 1 and the remaining loss components are equivalent.

E1.justification: v2 adds full ImageNet evaluation with street-sign, traffic-light, and giant-lizard sensitive classes, substantially extending coverage beyond Imagenette's ten-class subset. Table 9 also expands CIFAR-10 sensitive-seed selections. CIFAR-10, Imagenette, and the binary benign-versus-malignant HAM10k task remain.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 and 6–7 add SmoothAdv, SmoothMix, SmoothAdv-R, and SmoothMix-R. HAM10k also gains SmoothAdv comparisons. Cohen and Cohen-R are renamed Gaussian and Gaussian-R. The radius-comparison analysis replaces MACER with Ours, while the Zhang–Evans comparison remains in Appendix C.

E3.justification: The reported usual reweighting choice changes from alpha=1.2 to 1.1, retaining the same search grid; this does not establish reruns. New experiments introduce ResNet-50 for ImageNet and averaging across selected cost matrices. Tables 1–2 omit standard-radius robustness diagnostics, while existing architectures, primary metrics, and principal noise/perturbation settings remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds frequencies and examples of the standard empirical radius exceeding the cost-sensitive estimate (Table 8), sensitivity to seed/target selection (Table 9), and classwise clean/robust error analysis (Figure 5). Trade-off comparisons and perturbation curves expand. Some hyperparameter sensitivity curves disappear, although the numerical tuning grid survives in Table 5.

E5.justification: Table 9 newly reports averages with ± values across cost-matrix selections. The meaning of ± is not defined, and no independent training-run counts or random seeds are supplied, so additional repeated runs cannot be inferred. The Monte Carlo certification confidence construction remains unchanged.

E6.justification: v2 adds ImageNet, new-baseline, and Appendix D.3 results and revises retained scores. At sigma=epsilon=0.25, Table 7 changes Ours' CIFAR-10 robustness from 83.6% to 93.5% for the single pair and 68.9% to 91.4% for multiple targets. HAM10k robustness changes from 41.3% to 42.7%. Standard-radius diagnostic entries and the separate HAM10k Cohen-R-II result are removed.

T1.justification: The certified-radius definitions, ordering result, and union-bound confidence proof retain their mathematical substance. v1 Theorems 3.3–3.4 become v2 Theorems 3.2–3.3, while v1 Theorem 3.2's certification statement remains in prose. The added remarks explain bound behavior without introducing a new formal theorem or proof.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a randomized-smoothing framework for certifying and training cost-sensitive robustness under binary cost matrices, with a favorable accuracy–robustness trade-off. The expanded experiments and certification discussion support these retained contributions rather than redefine their central scope.

C2.justification: v2 explains when the standard empirical bound can outperform the cost-sensitive estimate and develops a class-level account of robustness redistribution, including increased dog-to-cat errors and the need for more balanced training. It also corrects swapped gamma interpretations in the tuning discussion and removes v1's speculative applicability discussion for other perturbation norms.

D1.justification: v2 discloses hardware and approximate per-setting runtimes: one 40GB A100 within a day for the smaller datasets, and four such GPUs over 1–2 days for ImageNet. Appendix B documents the added reweighting adaptations. The implementation URL is unchanged and merely moves from the availability section to the abstract.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including SmoothMix, ImageNet, Carmon et al., and Szegedy et al., while shortening the cost-sensitive robustness survey and removing other-norm references. The adversarially trained smoothing discussion changes attribution from Shafahi to Salman. The principal positioning against standard smoothing and convex-relaxation certification remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions, related work, and certification narrative are extensively rewritten. Evaluation metrics move into the experiments section; reweighting methods and the convex-relaxation comparison move into appendices. Proofs and supplementary experiments are regrouped, and terminology and notation are systematically revised.

P2.justification: Most experimental tables are restructured with datasets and settings grouped into columns, and HAM10k results are combined with ImageNet. Certification curves are redistributed, trade-off panels are expanded, and hyperparameter plots are condensed. Tables 8–9 and the four-panel heatmap Figure 5 are new.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the previously limited evidence for scalability and comparative effectiveness through full ImageNet evaluation and adversarial-training/mixup baselines. Appendix analyses also expose class-level costs and dependence on cost-matrix selection. These gains outweigh the loss of diagnostic entries, although undefined ± values and blanket superiority wording remain weaknesses: Table 1's CIFAR-10 M-Seed (2,4) results actually favor SmoothAdv-R over Ours.
